title: Giving Vulnerable Parents a Voice: A Qualitative Synthesis Review of Parent Engagement Experience in Child Maltreatment Prevention Programs
abstract: Recent child welfare policies in the United States prioritize child maltreatment prevention, making parent engagement in voluntary prevention services crucial to program effectiveness. However, engaging parents in high-risk families remains a significant challenge. This qualitative synthesis review examines parents’ perspectives on factors influencing their engagement and identifies parent-recommended strategies to enhance engagement. A systematic search of multiple databases yielded 3,447 studies published between 1980 and 2022. Fifty-three peer-reviewed qualitative and mixed-methods studies published between 1991 and 2022 that explored parent engagement experiences in child maltreatment prevention programs met the inclusion criteria. We assessed study quality using the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme tool and synthesized qualitative findings using thematic analysis. The qualitative synthesis identified three major domains influencing parent engagement: factors shaping parent engagement, engagement experiences, and parent-recommended strategies. Parents engaged more successfully when programs addressed contextual, internal, and external factors, including socioeconomic adversity, motivation, practical resources, program design, and provider relationships. Positive engagement fostered trust, support, parenting confidence, and stronger family relationships, whereas judgment, cultural mismatch, provider inconsistency, and logistical barriers hindered engagement. Parents recommended culturally responsive and father-inclusive services, flexible program delivery, practical supports, and strong provider-parent partnerships to strengthen engagement. Parent engagement in child maltreatment prevention programs is a dynamic process shaped by interactions among individual, programmatic, and broader contextual factors. Building trusting relationships, reducing structural barriers, and incorporating parents’ perspectives into program design and delivery are essential for strengthening engagement and improving the effectiveness of child maltreatment prevention services.
